Screens, new — Rich Docs

Docs states

Everything that can go differently from the good path in the new Docs: loading, converting, saving, offline and reconnecting, two people editing, a session that ended, no access, deleted and missing pages, limits, blocked embeds, unsupported browsers, read-only roles, an AI team at work on the page, search, keyboard and screen reader use, and dark mode. Sample project: Kanban Board (KAN).
A
Loading
A page and its tree load on their own. The skeleton follows the real shape of a rich page: a cover, a centred title, text, a picture beside text, a table. After 8 seconds a note and Retry appear and the skeleton stays; if the server does not answer, the page shows what happened and nothing is lost. Pressing Edit shows the page at once and fills the tools in as they arrive.
1. Desktop — Tree and page load separately; the page keeps its width and its picture-beside-text shape so nothing jumps.

CHAPTER THREE
The Salt Road

Nobody in Linh Dien remembered who had first called it the salt road, though everyone agreed it had never carried much salt. It ran north out of the village between two rows of drowned mangroves, and in the dry months the mud on either side cracked into plates the colour of old bread.1 Her grandmother had walked it every spring with a basket on her head and a story for each bend, and Mai had grown up believing that a road was only a long way of telling something.

By the time the ferry horn sounded across the flats she had already counted the posts twice. Forty-one, the same as yesterday, and the same as the year the floods came. The ferryman, who had once been a schoolteacher, liked to say that the village was the only place in the delta where the water kept better time than the clocks.

1 The dry season at Linh Dien runs from November to April; see the survey notes in Chapter One.

A page being converted
Pages written as Markdown are converted to the rich format one by one, in the background, the first time the new Docs is on. A page that is being converted can be read from its saved copy and cannot be edited yet; the tree shows how far the whole space is. If one page cannot be converted, its original text is kept, shown read-only, and an admin can be told.

Rate limiting

Published · v15HMEdited by Hoa Mai · 2h ago

Overview

Every route counts requests per token in a sliding one-minute window. When a token goes over its limit the API answers 429 with a Retry-After header. See Auth for how tokens are issued.

Rate limits are not enforced yet. Tracked in KAN-12.

ENGINEERING NOTES
What a year of weekly releases taught us
HMHoa Mai·12 Nov 2026·8 min read

When we moved from monthly to weekly releases last autumn, the first thing that changed was not the code. It was the Fridays. They became calmer than they had been in years, and nobody could quite say why until we counted the incidents.

Smaller batches, calmer Fridays

Release train, week 14: the board that replaced our monthly checklist.

A monthly release carried about sixty tickets. A weekly one carries fourteen. When something breaks, the list of suspects is short enough to read out loud in a stand-up, and the rollback is a single revert instead of an archaeology project.

We kept the same checks, the same reviewers and the same board. What went away was the release freeze, the Thursday night spreadsheet and the quiet dread.

Nobody is afraid of a release that is only forty lines long.
Tuan Vo, on the first Friday we shipped before lunch

What the numbers said

Over the year we shipped 51 releases. Rollbacks fell from nine to two, and the median time from merge to production dropped to under four hours.

Rules
The queue is per page and per browser.
Changes are sent in the order made; a picture waits, the text does not.
Publishing and sharing always need a connection.
E
Two people edit the same page
Most edits never meet: changes to different blocks are joined by themselves and the person is told. Only when both changed the same block is Publish paused, and the choice is made block by block: each side is drawn as it will look, text changes are underlined and struck, and a changed alignment or picture position is a plain label. View their changes, Keep mine and Reload stay as they are.

CHAPTER THREE
The Salt Road

Nobody in Linh Dien remembered who had first called it the salt road, though everyone agreed it had never carried much salt. It ran north out of the village between two rows of drowned mangroves, and in the dry months the mud on either side cracked into plates the colour of old bread.1 Her grandmother had walked it every spring with a basket on her head and a story for each bend, and Mai had grown up believing that a road was only a long way of telling something.

By the time the ferry horn sounded across the flats she had already counted the posts twice. Forty-one, the same as yesterday, and the same as the year the floods came. The ferryman, who had once been a schoolteacher, liked to say that the village was the only place in the delta where the water kept better time than the clocks.

1 The dry season at Linh Dien runs from November to April; see the survey notes in Chapter One.

ENGINEERING NOTES
What a year of weekly releases taught us
HMHoa Mai·12 Nov 2026·8 min read

When we moved from monthly to weekly releases last autumn, the first thing that changed was not the code. It was the Fridays. They became calmer than they had been in years, and nobody could quite say why until we counted the incidents.

Smaller batches, calmer Fridays

Release train, week 14: the board that replaced our monthly checklist.

A monthly release carried about sixty tickets. A weekly one carries fourteen. When something breaks, the list of suspects is short enough to read out loud in a stand-up, and the rollback is a single revert instead of an archaeology project.

We kept the same checks, the same reviewers and the same board. What went away was the release freeze, the Thursday night spreadsheet and the quiet dread.

Nobody is afraid of a release that is only forty lines long.
Tuan Vo, on the first Friday we shipped before lunch

What the numbers said

Over the year we shipped 51 releases. Rollbacks fell from nine to two, and the median time from merge to production dropped to under four hours.

Rate limiting

Published · v15HMEdited by Hoa Mai · 2h ago

Overview

Every route counts requests per token in a sliding one-minute window. When a token goes over its limit the API answers 429 with a Retry-After header. See Auth for how tokens are issued.

Rate limits are not enforced yet. Tracked in KAN-12.

K
Dark mode (proposal)
Proposal: the app has no dark theme today, so this is what one could look like. If it exists, the editor and the reader go dark together: the chrome, the bars, the dialogs and the page. The page keeps its own colours as far as they stay readable; named colours take their dark values, and a colour that fails contrast on the dark page gets the same warning as on a light one. Warnings and banners keep their meaning by icon and word, not only by colour.

CHAPTER THREE
The Salt Road

Nobody in Linh Dien remembered who had first called it the salt road, though everyone agreed it had never carried much salt. It ran north out of the village between two rows of drowned mangroves, and in the dry months the mud on either side cracked into plates the colour of old bread.1 Her grandmother had walked it every spring with a basket on her head and a story for each bend, and Mai had grown up believing that a road was only a long way of telling something.

By the time the ferry horn sounded across the flats she had already counted the posts twice. Forty-one, the same as yesterday, and the same as the year the floods came. The ferryman, who had once been a schoolteacher, liked to say that the village was the only place in the delta where the water kept better time than the clocks.

1 The dry season at Linh Dien runs from November to April; see the survey notes in Chapter One.

What a year of weekly releases…

ENGINEERING NOTES
What a year of weekly releases taught us
HMHoa Mai·12 Nov 2026·8 min read

When we moved from monthly to weekly releases last autumn, the first thing that changed was not the code. It was the Fridays. They became calmer than they had been in years, and nobody could quite say why until we counted the incidents.

Smaller batches, calmer Fridays

Release train, week 14: the board that replaced our monthly checklist.

A monthly release carried about sixty tickets. A weekly one carries fourteen. When something breaks, the list of suspects is short enough to read out loud in a stand-up, and the rollback is a single revert instead of an archaeology project.

We kept the same checks, the same reviewers and the same board. What went away was the release freeze, the Thursday night spreadsheet and the quiet dread.

Nobody is afraid of a release that is only forty lines long.
Tuan Vo, on the first Friday we shipped before lunch

What the numbers said

Over the year we shipped 51 releases. Rollbacks fell from nine to two, and the median time from merge to production dropped to under four hours.
